hints: Focus on the typical laboratory conditions for each reaction type, especially which ones always need heat, reflux or concentrated acid.
Remember that $\text{PCl}_5$ is a very vigorous chlorinating agent that fizzes instantly with an alcohol even in the cold.
Compare that instant room temperature test with nitrile formation, dehydration to an alkene, and nitrile hydrolysis, all of which need prolonged heating to work.
walkthrough:
**Sort reactions by energy demand**

Think like a lab chemist. Most substitutions, eliminations and hydrolyses have high activation energy, so we heat under reflux. Only a few very exothermic reagents work in the cold.

General idea:
$$\text{cold and fast} = \text{very reactive reagent, low } E_a$$

**Recall the standard conditions**

$\text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{PCl}_5$ is the classic test for $\text{-OH}$. It is vigorous at room temperature and gives steamy white fumes of $\text{HCl}$.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{PCl}_5 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} + \text{POCl}_3 + \text{HCl}$$

**Check the other three**

B is nucleophilic substitution by $\text{CN}^-$ to extend the chain. It needs heating under reflux in ethanol.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{KCN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{KBr}$$
C is dehydration of ethanol to ethene. It needs concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ and strong heating, about $170^{\circ}\text{C}$.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
D is acid or alkaline hydrolysis of a nitrile. It needs boiling under reflux with dilute $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{NaOH}$.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_3$$
Only the alcohol with $\text{PCl}_5$ is quick at $20^{\circ}\text{C}$.

options.A: Correct. Primary alcohols react rapidly and exothermically with $\text{PCl}_5$ at room temperature with no heating. You see vigorous fizzing and white fumes of $\text{HCl}$, forming $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ and $\text{POCl}_3$. This is why it is used as a cold chemical test for the $\text{-OH}$ group.
options.B: Incorrect. Reaction of a bromoalkane with $\text{KCN}$ in ethanol is nucleophilic substitution to make a nitrile. It is slow in the cold and must be heated under reflux to give the $\text{CN}^-$ ion enough energy to displace $\text{Br}^-$ in reasonable time.
options.C: Incorrect. Dehydration of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to ethene is an elimination that needs concentrated sulfuric or phosphoric acid catalyst and strong heating. At $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ with no acid shown, essentially nothing happens.
options.D: Incorrect. Hydrolysis of a nitrile to a carboxylic acid breaks very strong $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ bonds. It requires boiling under reflux for a long time with dilute aqueous acid or alkali. It does not occur quickly at room temperature.
